title: Cold Call (You Need a System)
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles argues that cold calling, the random sampling of students via lollipop sticks, only changes outcomes when schools give teachers a system that turns it into habit. He grounds the case in retrieval and the testing effect, then makes a professional-development argument of his own: after eight years as an assistant head he concluded that follow-up, not the quality of the launch training, determines whether practice changes. His Pareto-style picture of a staff has about 20 percent who adopt at once, 20 percent who resist, and 60 percent who can be swayed if a prop makes consistency easy. A scripted coaching conversation then prices the time wasted choosing names and extrapolates to extra marks and grades. It is a persuasive, if back-of-envelope, case that implementation support beats inspirational training.
points: Cold call works because random selection makes every student expect to be asked, so more of them retrieve and think before a name is called.
Salles's Pareto principle of CPD holds that a launch session wins about 20 percent immediately, loses another 20 percent to resistance, and leaves the persuadable 60 percent to follow-up.
A physical system such as names on lollipop sticks removes the decision cost of choosing whom to ask, which is what makes the habit automatic.
His time arithmetic, about 14 hours of reclaimed teaching across KS4, is illustrative rather than rigorous, but it frames small routines as large cumulative gains.
quotes: Cold call tests memory. The testing effect builds long term memory. A random approach to questioning makes more students imagine ‘it might be me’ and think about your question before you name the person who will answer it.

Your brilliant teaching doesn’t make your students remember what you’ve taught them. They’ll remember you, and that you were inspirational, motivational, entertaining and an all round good egg. But, if you don’t have ways of making them remember what you’ve taught, where has it got them?

But, over the course of 8 years I increasingly realised this was flawed thinking. The quality of my delivery made little difference to the likelihood of training having an impact on later practice. What mattered was the follow up.
20% of teachers will buy in immediately. They will do 80% of the cold calling in the school.

But, doing Cold Call takes more than knowing it is better teaching. It is a change of habit, which is always hard. A system will make it easy for you - it will make Cold Call automatic, so a much easier habit to acquire.
If we wait 10 seconds for each name choice without the lollipop, that’s 3 minutes and 20 seconds of your lesson lost. If you teach 7 lessons a fortnight, that’s 22 minutes and 10 seconds.
Ok, about a third of your class would get a higher grade. All it takes is a set of lollipop sticks.
